subject: On ggvis' usefulness (or lack thereof) and how it could be improved

messages.author: c1cb392dfeeacea0
messages.subject: On ggvis' usefulness (or lack thereof) and how it could be improved
parts:
Alas after a quick evaluation yesterday, I have a few critical comments to make about ggvis in an interactive environment. Insofar what you guys have is more or less a web clone of ggplot2, which isn't all that useful in the web world of 2014. To be useful in a interactive environment for exploratory analysis you need at least:

1) Good auto-generated tooltips [for highlighting etc.], which means x,y values and every factor that's in the vis ["layer"] by default. Sure, add a programmatic way [hooks] to change/tweak them, but don't make me program the tooltips ever time.

2) An easy, interactive way to add/remove levels of a factor to a visualization. At least an auto-generated radio buttons list, possibly add multiple range selection for continuous ones [on heat maps] etc. You have a interval widget that one could use for a single interval, but for multiple continuous intervals, I'm not even sure how to do it [using your widget set] without overloading the UI.

Note that even Excel's pivot chart can do add/remove of factor levels with a click [since the 2010 version has added "slicers"]. Moving factors between axes with drag-and-drop [which Excel also does] isn't that important in practice IMO, but it's sometimes handy. Being able map to factor to colors or shapes is more important in my book, but the brains of Microsoft apparently don't grok that, so Excel only does some useless theming with the colors in most pivot chart types because it still lacks a sufficiently general notion of binding data to an visual element in the graph, unlike stuff based on Gramar of Graphics.

And if you don't want to take the word of an anonymous dog on the Internet (I can't remove the virtual paper bag from my virtual head for good reasons), look at recommendations for interactivity on p. 27 in Tableau Software's guidebook http://mkt.tableausoftware.com/files/VisualGuidebookTabRead.pdf. They mention the first two points at least. 

3) And the final ingredient for a good interactive visualization is a good animation when you do certain kinds of filtering changes. This is really important when a data set is bigger than 100 displayed points or so. Human vision is sensitive to motion but can't diff easily in the brain instant changes (aka the famous "change blindness"). Motion charts are based on this idea for time series, but you can use it for non-time data to explore "what if" and filter scenarios in almost any kind of data. I've done filterable Sunburst charts for example which were well received. (Alas I can't share the code because my employer doesn't see any benefit in that.)

Alas your chosen interposer/middleware, Vega, doesn't seem to even have a clue what animation is, even though D3 itself underneath isn't that clueless. Perhaps that happens because the theoretical model of Grammar of Graphics doesn't include any notion of interaction [like tooltips] or animation; I guess an extension in that direction would be a fairly good research topic.

I can't close this topic without mentioning that poor animation performance is still a big issue in the web world. So choose your poison wisely in this regard... I for one prefer[ed] to use JIT (JavaScript InfoVist Toolkit) over D3 for anything involving animation because of the performance issue. I can write a big brain dump about the finer points of [charts/visualization] animation with web technologies, but I'm not sure anyone on this list would want to read it... given the complete lack of such support in ggvis. In 2014 however, I'm very weary of choosing any sort of interposer/middleware that can't output WebGL directly [after IE11 adopted it in surprise move], although any middleware you chose should have a fallback backend renderer [canvas/SVG] for older/crappy browsers, of course. I'd like to see an R charting package that does 3D directly via WebGL, which would also give awesome 2D [animation] performance. The guy that wrote JIT [for 2D] later wrote PhiloGL [for 3D], which you can see in action in demos like http://www.senchalabs.org/philogl/PhiloGL/examples/worldFlights/, although I have not yet used PhiloGL myself for any project yet. There's an attempt to marry D3 with WebGL known as PathGL, but it doesn't look well done, e.g. http://pathgl.com/examples/map.html is a rather poor demo.

These two features seem like an extremely limited definition of
interactive graphics to me, and they're certainly not a focus of
ggvis. You can implement both yourself (with a little code), and
certainly ggvis will get better at these two things out of the box,
but they're unlikely to be a development priority for some time.

> 3) And the final ingredient for a good interactive visualization is a good

> vision is sensitive to motion but can't diff easily in the brain instant

> if" and filter scenarios in almost any kind of data. I've done filterable

> the code because my employer doesn't see any benefit in that.)

It's really hard to know what you mean by "good animation" without any
additional description.

> however, I'm very weary of choosing any sort of interposer/middleware that
> can't output WebGL directly [after IE11 adopted it in surprise move],
> although any middleware you chose should have a fallback backend renderer
> [canvas/SVG] for older/crappy browsers, of course. I'd like to see an R
> charting package that does 3D directly via WebGL, which would also give
> awesome 2D [animation] performance. The guy that wrote JIT [for 2D] later
> wrote PhiloGL [for 3D], which you can see in action in demos like
> http://www.senchalabs.org/philogl/PhiloGL/examples/worldFlights/, although I
> have not yet used PhiloGL myself for any project yet. There's an attempt to
> marry D3 with WebGL known as PathGL, but it doesn't look well done, e.g.
> http://pathgl.com/examples/map.html is a rather poor demo.

Vega is a completely different beast to JIT. JIT gives you a canned
set of visualisations (a typology) that it does really well. Vega, and
ggvis, gives you a set of building blocks that allows you to tailor
visualisations to your needs. Our current priority is expressiveness,
not performance. We have planned some time in the future to look at
performance optimisations, and using webgl to render is an obvious
place to look (although it brings with its own set of problems, like
rendering text well).
